analysis.one_liner: Bars federal agencies from issuing any costly new rule unless they repeal existing rules of equal or greater cost.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees, sent to a subcommittee, and never received a vote before the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every federal agency, before issuing any new rule that costs money for businesses, individuals, or state and local governments, to first repeal or revise existing rules costing at least as much. The White House budget office would have to certify that each new rule's cost did not exceed the cost of the rules it replaced. In effect, it would have frozen the total cost of federal regulation: agencies could only add a new safety, health, consumer, or environmental protection by cutting an equally expensive one somewhere else.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses and other regulated entities gain the most, because the bill caps the total cost they can be made to bear: a new rule could only be issued if an equal-cost rule were repealed, so their cumulative compliance costs could not grow. State and local governments, which are covered by the bill when rules impose responsibilities on them, would also see fewer new federal mandates. Supporters argue consumers benefit indirectly when compliance savings are passed on in prices.

how_it_helps.text: Prevents agencies from stacking new compliance costs on regulated entities: no rule imposing costs on a nongovernmental person or a state or local government could be issued unless the agency repealed or revised related rules in a way that reduces costs to those entities.

Requires that the cost of any new rule be less than or equal to the cost of the rules repealed or revised, with the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs certifying the cost comparison before the rule is issued.
Requires every rule repealed or revised under the offset requirement to be published in the Federal Register, making the trade-offs visible to the public.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people pay in protections foregone. Under the bill, a new workplace safety standard, food or drug safety rule, consumer protection, or environmental safeguard could only be issued if an equally costly existing rule were cut first. Because the bill measures only costs, not the benefits of rules, agencies would be forced to weigh protections against a hard budget cap regardless of how much good a rule would do.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone who relies on federal protections

drawbacks.text: The bill counts only what rules cost regulated parties, not what they deliver: a rule preventing workplace deaths or foodborne illness receives no credit for its benefits, so agencies would be structurally biased against issuing protective rules even where benefits far exceed costs.

The offset applies to any rule imposing a cost or responsibility on a nongovernmental person or a state or local government, with no exception for emergencies or urgent public health and safety rules, and certification is required before the rule can be issued.

An honest supporter would acknowledge that a rigid one-for-one cap makes no distinction between a well-designed rule and a wasteful one on the other side of the ledger: an agency could satisfy the requirement by cutting an important rule instead of a trivial one.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit to the public rests on an assumption — that cutting other regulations saves consumers more than the new rule would protect them — and the bill includes no mechanism to test it, since only costs are measured. The cost falls on anyone who would have been protected by future rules, because every new protection would require tearing down an existing one of equal expense. It is a blunt instrument aimed at a real complaint (cumulative regulatory burden) that would have constrained agencies even where regulation clearly pays for itself.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee: after being referred to two House committees and then to a Judiciary subcommittee, no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened, and the bill died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael McCaul introduced the One In, One Out Act in the House on July 28, 2015, joined by eight Republican cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform and to the Committee on the Judiciary on the day it was introduced.
On September 8, 2015, the House Judiciary Committee referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law.
No further action was recorded before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, so the bill never reached the House floor and never became law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people kept the status quo: agencies retained full freedom to issue new protections without an offset requirement, and regulated industries did not get the cost cap they sought. Nothing changed for anyone.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Anyone counting on future federal rules

against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law on September 8, 2015, and never reported it out or scheduled a markup.

against.role: Committee of referral; chair Rep. Jason Chaffetz (R)

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was entirely Republican — Rep. McCaul plus eight GOP cosponsors, with no Democratic cosponsors — but the bill never came to a vote, so where the broader chambers stood was never tested.

industries.industry: Regulated businesses (manufacturers, energy, financial firms, and other industries subject to federal rules)
industries.note: The bill would have capped the total cost these entities can be made to bear by requiring equal-cost repeal of existing rules before any new costly rule is issued. Their gain comes at the expense of the public's future protections, since agencies could not add a rule without cutting one of equal cost.

Rules imposing responsibilities on states and localities are covered by the offset requirement, so governments would face fewer new federal mandates. The benefit depends on which rules get cut, which could also remove protections those governments rely on.

Agencies would lose discretion: every new costly rule would require an offset and pre-issuance certification by the White House regulatory office. Agencies could argue this forces better prioritization, but it also constrains them by formula.
